solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Rat-arsed I with claret, object!

indicators.note: rat-arsed is crude slang for blind drunk, so the words that follow stagger out of order

explanation.surface: A drunk protests as someone pairs him with a bottle of red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object!' looks like an outburst of protest, but it is the noun meaning a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: An article is a thing or item, and an object is likewise a physical thing.

clue.text: (& 20dn.) Each emerging fiasco that Obama says he's not aiming for in the Middle East

definitions.text: that Obama says he's not aiming for in the Middle East

indicators.note: a fiasco is a shambles, so the preceding words come out in a jumbled state

explanation.surface: Every fresh Middle East disaster is the very outcome the US president insists he is not seeking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emerging' reads as a verb describing the fiasco, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Obama repeatedly said his Syria and Libya policies did not seek the overthrow of governments, which is what removing a ruling administration means.

clue.text: Aggressive, hot equerry finally hits Brenda with mug

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the courtier's title, the only part kept

blocks.note: hot in the sense of fashionable, in vogue
Private Eye's nickname for the late Queen, whose royal cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A furious royal attendant strikes the Queen with a drinking mug.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so she stands for ER, Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: In-yer-face is slang for something confrontational and blatant, pushed right at people, which is what aggressive behaviour does.

clue.text: Like Tim Rice breaks the heart of Julian Clary?

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle pair of letters of the first name is used
something broken is smashed up, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: the two central letters of Julian

explanation.surface: Is a famous lyricist so charming that he breaks the comedian Julian Clary's heart?
explanation.walkthrough: Tim Rice wrote the words for Jesus Christ Superstar and Evita; Julian Clary is a camp British comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: Tim Rice is a celebrated writer of song words, so being like him means being given to writing song words or poetic expression.

clue.text: Crusty southern sort who has celebs in the back?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern

blocks.clueFragment: sort who has celebs in the back?
blocks.note: a taxi driver carries famous passengers on the rear seat

explanation.surface: A gruff southerner seems to be some kind of celebrity hanger-on with stars stashed behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: The second part is a little cryptic definition: the person with celebrities in the back is a London taxi driver.
explanation.definitionFit: Scabby skin is covered with dried crusts over healing sores, so crusty is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Singular ageing singer, holding them up vulgarly, who has a wheeze

indicators.note: holding means gripping something within, so the singer's name is wrapped around the short pronoun

blocks.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
'em is the colloquial clipped form of them; up merely completes the phrase holding up

explanation.surface: A veteran diva props up a crowd in a crude way while wheezing herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheeze' suggests breathlessness from an ageing singer, but in British slang a wheeze is a clever scheme or dodge.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheeze is British slang for a crafty plan, so a person who has one is plotting, a plotter.

clue.text: One has-been Labour leader to make a comeback? No earthly!

indicators.note: a comeback sends something back the way it came, so the leader's name is read from the end

blocks.note: Neil Kinnock, Labour leader in the 1980s

explanation.surface: Will a washed-up former Labour leader return to front-line politics? Not a chance on earth!
explanation.walkthrough: 'No earthly' sounds like the idiom 'not an earthly chance', but here it describes something not from Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A being from another planet is not of this world, so it is literally not earthly.

clue.text: The two taking in Cyclops, the man with erection: "monstrous thing!"

indicators.note: in a down light an erection points the letters upward, so they are read from the bottom
taking in means admitting inside, so the pair word surrounds the other letters

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: Two people meet the setter and an aroused man and cry out at the monstrosity.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often clue themselves as ME, here by their pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A behemoth is the huge biblical beast, and by extension any enormous creature or monster.

clue.text: (& 13ac.) Spin tip: go back on yourself

blocks.note: the tail is the end or tip of something

explanation.surface: A spin doctor's advice: reverse your own position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin tip' reads as political PR advice, but the two words simply give the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn tail is to retreat in fright, wheeling round and heading back the way you came.

clue.text: As Ed Miliband under attack became, say, a gutless bloke

definitions.text: As Ed Miliband under attack became

indicators.note: gutless means with the insides removed, so only the outside letters of the bloke remain

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, as does say
a bloke is a guy; keep only its outer letters

explanation.surface: A spineless chap describes how the Labour leader fared when assailed.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2014 Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, was hit by an egg thrown during a walkabout.
explanation.definitionFit: Being pelted with eggs leaves you smeared in yolk, so the egged politician ended up covered in egg, egg-coated.

clue.text: Through gin, screwed around – and not a wink's sleep?

indicators.note: screwed around means messed about with, so the preceding letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone drank gin and slept around, and then could not sleep at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Through' looks like a preposition, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough night is an idiom for a bad night with little or no rest.

clue.text: (& 22dn.) A nation's aspirational vision - to bomb the 'bad guys'?

blocks.note: first meaning: the ideal of prosperity open to every citizen of the USA
second meaning, satirical: what the US apparently ... of doing abroad

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a jibe at US foreign policy, treating air strikes on villains as the country's real fantasy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the national ideal of success through effort, and the satirical second reading twists it into a fantasy of military action.

clue.text: Cyclops is going back and forth guarding the last bit of erection, note

indicators.note: going back then forth means the short phrase is written once backwards and once forwards
the last bit of a word is its final letter alone
guarding means standing round something to protect it, so the doubled letters enclose the single one

blocks.note: the setter is: I'm, here the copy that goes back
I'm again, the copy that goes forth

explanation.surface: The setter paces to and fro protecting what is left of an erection, take note.
explanation.definitionFit: A minim is a musical note worth two crotchets, called a half note in American usage.

clue.text: see 8dn.
Viciousness for ruined, drug-taking bankers and financiers

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the short preposition is broken up and rebuilt
taking means swallowing something inside, as a user takes a pill

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
the City is London's financial district and the people working there

explanation.surface: The savagery of City bankers, wrecked by their drug habits.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is the Square Mile of London, home to its banks, so it stands for financiers as a group.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferocity is fierceness or savage cruelty, a near synonym of viciousness.

clue.text: see 25ac.
Taking monetary advantage of old Eurosceptic getting in drink

blocks.note: Sir Bill Cash, veteran Conservative Eurosceptic MP

explanation.surface: A veteran anti-EU politician profits by getting a round in.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Cash was a long-serving Tory MP famed for opposing the European Union.
explanation.definitionFit: To cash in on something is an idiom for exploiting it for profit or gain.

clue.text: On which one may lie about Clegg's chief row with right

indicators.note: the chief letter of a name is the one at its head, its first

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg's dispute with the right is something he might tell fibs about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' hints at politicians' dishonesty, but here it means to recline.
explanation.definitionFit: A recliner is an armchair whose back tilts so a person can lie back in it.

clue.text: One who gives a shit, not a rat

indicators.note: not here means without, so the following letter is struck out

explanation.surface: Someone who actually cares, unlike a treacherous type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives a shit' reads as caring, but is taken literally here.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat is slang for a traitor who deserts their side, which is what someone who switches allegiance does.

clue.text: Speaker who sends indiscreet messages to one and all?

definitions.text: Speaker who sends indiscreet messages to one and all?

blocks.clueFragment: Speaker who sends indiscreet messages to one and all?
blocks.note: surface reading: a gossip who blabs secrets to everyone

blocks.clueFragment: Speaker who sends indiscreet messages to one and all?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a pioneering orbiting relay whose name suggests one that tells, beaming broadcasts to the whole world

explanation.walkthrough: The name was given to the first communications satellite of 1962, and it splits into a tell-tale and a celestial body; indiscreet points to telling.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1962 satellite relayed television and telephone signals across the Atlantic, broadcasting to everyone, while its name suggests one who tells.

clue.text: Hot, topless ex-leader's gag

indicators.note: topless means with the head removed, so the name loses its opening letter

blocks.note: H for hot, as on a tap
George W Bush, former US president

explanation.surface: A former president shown topless in the heat becomes the butt of a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a joke, but here it means silencing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To gag someone is to stop them speaking, and hush likewise means to silence or quieten.

clue.text: Elevate dukes' position and push off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Promote some aristocrats and then tell them to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Push off' reads as a rude dismissal, but off is the signal to rearrange. Dukes is old slang for fists.
explanation.definitionFit: Dukes is slang for fists, so raising them puts the arms in the raised-palms stance a gunman demands.

clue.text: see 2dn.
"Balls' focus on shifty deal" scoop

indicators.note: the focus of a word is its centre point, its middle letter
shifty suggests shifting about, so the following letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline exposing Ed Balls' preoccupation with a dodgy deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was Labour's shadow chancellor. The scoop is spelt LADLE; this grid copies a misspelling, and the same letters fit either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladle is a long-handled deep spoon for serving soup, used to scoop liquid out of a pot.

clue.text: see 11ac.
Lead exchange – "good sort of fun," pissed leader goes

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version, so the short word is rearranged
when the leader goes, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A drunken party leader is ousted after a jolly exchange of views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like the verb to guide, but it is the metal of bullets.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunfight is an exchange of shots, and bullets are traditionally made of lead.

clue.text: see 25ac.
Popular with head of Finance, shocking treatment on debts that can be spread

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: electroconvulsive therapy, treatment by electric shock
IOUs are written acknowledgements of debt

explanation.surface: A finance chief applauded for harsh measures on debt, which might spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shocking treatment' sounds like scandalous handling of debts, but it means ECT, electric shock therapy.
explanation.definitionFit: An infectious disease is one passed from person to person, so it can spread.

clue.text: (& 14dn/23dn.) Spent, hapless president full of slush – don't expect a comeback

indicators.note: full of means filled with, so the president's name is packed around the slush

blocks.note: Gerald Ford, US president known for clumsiness

explanation.surface: A worn-out, gaffe-prone president full of sentimental mush will not return to office.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerald Ford was mocked for stumbles and gaffes, and lost the 1976 election.
explanation.definitionFit: Gone for good means permanently departed, so whoever has left will not be returning.

clue.text: Bit of a shake up from first pair of transvestites to take Catholic church over

indicators.note: the first pair of a word is its opening two letters
turned over means flipped, so the church's name is read backwards

blocks.note: the Roman Catholic Church is often called Rome

explanation.surface: Cross-dressers seize the Catholic Church in a minor upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rome' as shorthand for the Catholic Church, like Canterbury for the Anglicans.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremor is a slight quake or trembling, a small shake rather than a big upheaval.

clue.text: Fibre gets e.g. Ling Ling almost into shagging

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter
into means going inside, so the shortened animal sits within the other word

blocks.note: Ling-Ling was a famous giant panda in Washington's National Zoo
shagging is British slang for having sex

explanation.surface: A synthetic fabric lures a famously reluctant zoo panda into mating.
explanation.walkthrough: Ling-Ling and her mate Hsing-Hsing were famous for zoo keepers' failed attempts to get them to breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Spandex is a stretchy synthetic material, an elastic fibre used in sportswear.
